[00:00:04] Operator: Thank you for sitting down with me, Margaret. I thought we'd start somewhere easy. You mentioned last week that you grew up near the river.
[00:00:19] Margaret: That's right. Bewdley. We were on the Severn side, in a little terrace on Lax Lane. My father worked the carpet mills at Kidderminster and he'd cycle it, six miles each way, in all weathers.
[00:00:41] Operator: What's the first place there you can still picture clearly?
[00:00:47] Margaret: The kitchen. Always the kitchen. There was a range that never went out, and my mother had a chair beside it that nobody else was allowed to sit in. Not because she said so. You just knew.
[00:01:09] Operator: What was her name?
[00:01:12] Margaret: Edith. Edith Mary Pargeter, before she married. She was born in 1908, so she'd have been about thirty when I came along.
[00:01:28] Operator: And you were born in?
[00:01:31] Margaret: 1938. March. Just before it all started, which my mother never stopped mentioning.
[00:01:44] Operator: Do you remember the war years at all?
[00:01:49] Margaret: Bits. I remember the evacuees more than the war, if I'm honest. We had two boys from Birmingham billeted with us, brothers, and the younger one cried every night for about a fortnight. Alan and Peter. I can't remember the surname now.
[00:02:16] Operator: What was that like for you?
[00:02:20] Margaret: I was furious. I'd had my own room and then I didn't. I was five, I think. Six. And I remember deciding I hated them, properly hated them, and then about three weeks in Peter gave me half his sweet ration without being asked and that was that. We wrote to each other until I was nineteen.
[00:03:01] Operator: Nineteen — what happened then?
[00:03:05] Margaret: I went to Worcester. There was a job at the Royal Infirmary, auxiliary nursing, and my father didn't want me to take it. He thought I'd be back inside six months. That was the closest we ever came to a real falling out.
[00:03:29] Operator: What did he say?
[00:03:32] Margaret: He said, "You'll not last a winter on those wards." Those exact words. And I didn't answer him, I just went. I stayed eleven years.
[00:03:51] Operator: Did he ever say anything about that afterwards?
[00:03:56] Margaret: Not in so many words. But when I got my certificate he drove over — and he'd never driven anywhere, he borrowed a car off the foreman — and he sat at the back and didn't say a thing and then took me for a fish supper afterwards. That was him saying it.
[00:04:28] Operator: That's a lovely thing to have.
[00:04:31] Margaret: He died two years later. Fifty-eight. So I'm glad of the fish supper.
[00:04:44] Operator: I'm sorry.
[00:04:47] Margaret: It was a long time ago now. You get to my age and it's all a long time ago.
[00:05:02] Operator: Can I ask about the hospital years? Eleven years is a long time.
[00:05:09] Margaret: It was. I met Ron there, of course. He was a porter, then he did his training. We married in 1962 at St Martin's and we had Susan the year after, then David in 1966.
[00:05:38] Operator: What was Ron like?
[00:05:42] Margaret: Quiet. Very quiet. People thought he was stern and he wasn't, he was shy, which is a different thing entirely. He'd do anything for anybody and never mention it. I found out years later he'd been paying a neighbour's coal bill through an entire winter and hadn't told me.
[00:06:15] Operator: How did you find out?
[00:06:18] Margaret: She told me at his funeral. Which was a very Ron way for me to find out.
